surfaces.part: ice floor tile patch (terrain, seen from above)

answer.evidence: The silhouette is a full 160px-wide rectangle across rows 0-111 with no change in width. It is a flat ice floor texture with cracks and frost patches. Rows 0-2 show a darker wall-contact shadow along the top, and a similar shadow runs along the left edge. There is no standing body, no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical south face. This matches the terrain kind, a flat floor tile seen from above, so it is a top-down surface with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate reads as a decent ice floor. It has about 5 blue steps (near-white, pale, light, mid and deeper blue), dithered hatching, crack lines and mottled patches. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the wall-contact shadow lines lean blue and count as dark material tone. The weakness is the large pale base areas, which are flat: 21% of pixels sit inside 5x5 single-colour blocks, while both references have 0%. Colour counts are also low. The median is 7 per tile, only matching the paving reference and far below the grass reference's 26. The candidate has 36 distinct colours against the grass reference's 80. The texture is concentrated in a few dithered patches and cracks instead of covering the surface like the grass tufts and paving stones do. Because of the flat-fill share and the lower richness, I rate it slightly under the Beodeul bar, and I fail it where there is doubt.

surfaces.part: ice floor slab (10x7 tiles, seen from above)

answer.evidence: The image is a full-bleed terrain tile, 160 px wide for all rows 0-111, with an ice texture of cracks and frost patches. Rows 0-2 and the left columns are a dark contact shadow from the wall, which matches the stated purpose. There is no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical south face. It is a flat floor patch with no standing volume, so it reads as a top-down slab, which is expected for floor terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 4 ice-blue lightness steps: pale highlight, light, mid and a darker blue for the cracks and patches. It has dithering, hatch strokes and crack lines, so the texture is real, but it is uneven. The measured facts put it between the two references. Its 7 colours per tile equal the paving reference and sit far below the grass reference's 26. Its 36 distinct colours are well under the grass reference's 80. Its 5x5 flat-fill coverage is 21%, against 0% for both references, so there are visible flat light-blue areas, especially along the right and bottom. The edge and contact-shadow pixels are 0% neutral, so they carry a blue tint rather than a black line, which fits dark_material_tone. Overall the patch is a decent ice surface but shallower than the grass reference: fewer steps, less grain, and flat patches in several places. When in doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: ice floor tile field (flat ground seen from above)

answer.evidence: The image is a full-bleed 160px-wide ice floor texture covering rows 0-111 with no silhouette change. Rows 0-2 on top and the left columns are a dark grey-blue wall contact shadow, as the name says. The rest is a continuous light-blue ice pattern with cracks and frost patches. There is no standing object, no front-edge line, no eave shadow, no ellipse and no front face. It is a terrain tile, so the standing-object top and front-face rules do not apply. It reads as a flat floor texture, which matches the terrain kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 5 pale-blue lightness steps: white highlights, light ice, mid blue, deeper blue patches and dark blue cracks. It uses dither and hatch textures, crack lines, and per-blob shading on the darker patches. No neutral black line is used: the cracks and the wall-shadow rows lean blue, and the measured 0% near-neutral dark edge pixels agrees. The median of 7 colours per tile equals the paving reference (7) but is well under the grass (26). Its 36 distinct colours are fewer than the grass (80), but it has more than the paving (7). The 21% flat-fill coverage is the weak point, since the references sit at 0%. Those flat areas are the broad pale ice fields between the dithered patches, and this is a moderate flaw. Overall it is a little thinner than the grass, but a careful artist would accept it next to the references. The shading is layered, the outlines are tinted, and the texture is visible, so it does not read as a sticker or a flat fill.

surfaces.part: ice floor patch (whole tile area, seen from above)

answer.evidence: The image is a full-bleed 160px-wide, 112-row terrain floor texture. It is a flat ice surface with cracks and frost patches. The top rows 0-2 and the left column are dark contact-shadow strips under the wall, as the name describes. There is no standing body, no front face and no edge line or eave. It is a terrain tile and not a standing object, so the top/front-face rules for standing objects do not apply. The kind (terrain) matches the drawing.

styleAnswer.evidence: The ice floor has about 4 light-blue steps: pale highlight, light, mid and a deeper blue patch tone. It has dithered patches and thin crack lines, so it is not wholly flat. Its 36 colours and median of 7 per tile are well below the grass reference (80 colours, 26 per tile) and only match the paving reference, which is a very limited 7-colour piece. The 21% flat-fill coverage is the main problem: the grass and paving references have 0%, and the candidate has wide plain light-blue areas with no grain or speckle. The outline is tinted blue (0% neutral dark edge pixels), so that part is fine. The wall contact shadow along the top and left is present but is a simple band. Overall the piece is cleanly made and reads as ice, but it is flatter and sparser than the grass reference, and the large flat regions would stand out next to a Beodeul ground.
